_about: A synthetic showcase corpus for the public demo. Every person, client, project and figure here is invented. No real data from any repository or personal vault appears in this file, which is what makes it safe to publish.
persona: Wren Okafor runs Halcyon Studio, a four-person design practice.

items.title: Meridian rebrand — kickoff notes
items.body:
Meridian want the whole identity reconsidered, not a logo refresh.

What came out of the room:
- The current wordmark tests badly at small sizes. Everyone in the room independently called it "muddy".
- Their audience skews technical. They want to read as precise rather than friendly.
- Budget is firm at 48000 and the date is not movable: the new site goes live alongside their annual report.

Open question nobody could answer: who signs off. Adaora thinks it is the board, Tomas thinks it is him. Until that is settled we are designing for an audience of unknown size.

items.title: Typography that survives being shrunk
items.body:
Collected from four years of redrawing marks that looked fine at 200px and fell apart at 16.

The counters go first. An 'e' with a tight counter fills in before anything else breaks, which is why a logo that reads as a blur at favicon size is almost always a counter problem and almost never a weight problem.

Stroke contrast is the second failure. High contrast reads as elegant on a poster and as broken on a phone, because the thin strokes drop below one pixel and the letter starts missing parts of itself.

The test that actually works: render at 16px, screenshot, blur by two pixels, and see whether you can still tell the word. If you cannot, no amount of hinting will save it.

items.title: Studio standup — week 36
items.body:
Short one. Halcyon is at capacity until the Meridian delivery clears.

Sam is blocked on the illustration set because the brief never specified whether these run on dark backgrounds. That is a fifteen minute answer that has cost four days.

We agreed to stop taking discovery calls until October. Three of the last five went nowhere and each one cost most of a day.

items.title: Why we stopped quoting hourly
items.body:
Hourly billing punishes the thing we are best at. When a problem that would have taken a junior three weeks takes me an afternoon because I have solved its shape before, hourly billing charges the client less for the better outcome.

Since switching to fixed scope the average project value went from 11200 to 26500 and the arguments about timesheets stopped entirely.

The honest cost: we now have to be much better at saying what is out of scope, in writing, before anything starts. Two projects went badly in the first year because we were vague and then resentful.

items.title: Contrast is not a checkbox
items.body:
A ratio of 4.5:1 is the floor for body text, not the target. Hitting it exactly means the text is legible to someone with normal vision in a quiet room and marginal for everyone else.

The measurement people get wrong: translucent panels. If your panel is rgba over a dark ground, the contrast is against the *flattened* colour, not against the token you typed. A colour that measures 5.8:1 against #0f061c can be 2.6:1 against what the eye actually receives once the panel is composited.

Flatten first, then measure. Every time.

items.title: Overnight bread, no starter
items.body:
500g strong white flour, 380g water, 10g salt, 2g instant yeast.

Mix until no dry flour remains, cover, leave on the counter for twelve to eighteen hours. The long cold ferment does what kneading does, which is why this works without any technique at all.

Tip out, fold in thirds twice, rest thirty minutes, bake in a covered pot at 230C for thirty minutes covered and fifteen uncovered.

The only part that matters: the pot must be preheated. Cold pot gives a pale flat loaf and no amount of extra time fixes it.

items.title: Lisbon, notes for next time
items.body:
Stay east of the centre. Alfama is beautiful and completely impassable with a suitcase.

The conference venue is a forty minute walk from anywhere you want to eat, which nobody mentions.

Book the Gulbenkian in advance. Walked up twice and got turned away twice.

items.title: Post-mortem: the Northwind site
items.body:
Delivered six weeks late and roughly 9000 over. Worth writing down why while it still stings.

The cause was not the design work, which was done on time. It was that we agreed to "a few content pages" without counting them. A few turned out to be forty-one, each with its own layout argument.

What we change: scope is counted, in a spreadsheet, before a number is quoted. If the client cannot tell us how many pages, the contract prices a page and we bill per page.

The part I got wrong personally: I knew by week three and said nothing until week seven because I did not want the conversation.

items.title: The four-pixel module
items.body:
Every measurement in the studio system is a multiple of four. Not because four is magic, but because a single module removes an entire category of decision.

Before: every gap was an argument. 14 or 16? 22 or 24? The answers were arbitrary and nobody could defend one over another, so the arguments never resolved.

After: 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 48. Six values, and the question becomes which of six rather than which of infinity.

The cost is that occasionally 18 really is right and you have to take 16 or 20 instead. Worth it.

items.title: What I actually finished this year
items.body:
Eleven books started, six finished. The pattern is obvious in hindsight: everything I finished I read in physical form, everything I abandoned was on a screen.

Not making a principle out of it. Just noting it.

items.title: Invoicing, the boring version that works
items.body:
Invoice on the first of the month for everything delivered in the previous month. Not on delivery, not on milestones, not when you remember.

Terms are fourteen days and the late fee is real and has been charged twice. Both clients paid on time forever afterwards.

The single largest improvement to cash flow was not chasing faster. It was invoicing on a schedule so predictable that the client's finance team could plan around it.

items.title: Dark interfaces, what I keep relearning
items.body:
Pure black is wrong. #000 against white text produces halation — the text appears to vibrate — and on OLED the transition to any lit pixel is abrupt enough to read as a hard edge.

A near-black with a colour cast reads as intentional. #010006 has a violet lean so slight you cannot name it, but a wash of violet over it looks like part of the same surface rather than a coloured sheet laid on grey.

Heavy borders are the other tell. On a dark interface a 1px #333 border around every panel reads as cheap immediately. Distinguish panels by luminance and a hairline, never by a border you can see from across the room.

And saturated colour is signal, never surface. Neon on three percent of the pixels lands. Neon on thirty percent is a headache.

items.title: First week checklist for a new designer
items.body:
Day one is accounts and the studio system, nothing else. Do not give anyone client work on day one; they will produce something to prove themselves and it will be wrong in ways that are expensive to unpick.

Day two to four: redraw an existing project from the brief without looking at what we shipped. Then compare. This teaches the house standard faster than any document.

Day five: a real task, small, with a deadline that does not matter.

items.title: Meridian — competitor audit
items.body:
Nine competitors reviewed. Seven use a geometric sans, six use blue, five use an abstract mark built from overlapping shapes.

The category has converged to the point of being indistinguishable. Covered the logos and asked four people to match them to the companies; best score was two out of nine.

That is the opportunity and I will be arguing for it: almost anything with a point of view will be distinguishable here, because the bar is on the floor.

items.title: Studio backup policy, such as it is
items.body:
Working files on the studio drive, synced. Archive to the external disk on the first of the month. Off-site copy quarterly, which in practice means when I remember, which in practice means twice a year.

This is not good enough and I know it. The failure mode that worries me is not disk death, it is silent corruption that syncs everywhere before anyone notices.

What would actually fix it: versioned snapshots that are not writable by the machine that made them.

items.title: The projects I regret taking
items.body:
All four share a tell. In each case the first conversation contained the phrase "we know roughly what we want, we just need someone to make it".

That sentence means the thinking has not been done and will now be done by us, unpaid, while being described as execution.

The ones that went well started with a question, not a specification.

items.title: Font licensing, in plain terms
items.body:
Desktop licence covers making the artwork. Web licence covers serving it. App licence covers embedding it. These are three purchases and clients consistently assume they are one.

Put the licence cost in the quote as a separate line. When it is buried in a total it looks like padding; when it is a line item with the foundry named, nobody has ever questioned it.

Meridian's chosen family runs 1800 for desktop and web at their traffic tier.

items.title: Redraw the Meridian wordmark at small sizes
items.body: Three weights, tested at 16px, 24px and favicon. Blur test on each.

items.title: Unblock Sam's illustration brief
items.body: Answer the dark-background question. Fifteen minutes of work that has cost four days.

items.title: Establish who signs off at Meridian
items.body: Adaora says the board. Tomas says Tomas. Until this is answered we are guessing.

items.title: Put Northwind in the portfolio anyway
items.body: It ran late and over, and the work is still the best thing we shipped this year.

items.title: Decide whether to hire a fourth designer
items.body: We are turning down work. That is either a signal to hire or a signal to raise prices, and I genuinely do not know which.

items.title: Write the studio system down
items.body: It exists in my head and in four years of files. That is not a system, that is a habit.

items.title: Respond to the Castleford RFP
items.body: Withdrawn. Sixty pages of requirements for a fixed fee of 6000.

items.title: Meridian — first round review
items.body: Three directions. Do not show a favourite.

items.body: Three days. The workshop track is the reason to go; the keynotes are all online afterwards.

items.body: The clearest explanation of why term frequency saturates rather than growing linearly.

items.title: Adaora Nwosu
items.body: Marketing director at Meridian. Decisive, reads everything, will tell you exactly what she thinks in the room rather than in an email three days later.

items.title: Tomas Lindqvist
items.body: Meridian's founder. Believes he is the final approver. May be right.

items.title: Sam Oyelaran
items.body: Illustration and motion at Halcyon. Fastest person here when the brief is clear and completely stuck when it is not.

items.title: Ines Carvalho
items.body: Runs everything at Halcyon that is not design. The reason the studio has not fallen over.

items.title: Ruth Anand
items.body: Northwind. Fair about the overrun, which she did not have to be.

items.title: Quick capture, no tags, no thought
items.body:
Ask Ruth whether Northwind ever used the alternate mark.

This is what capture looks like when you are walking: a sentence, no tags, no kind chosen, sorted out later or never. It still turns up in search, which is the whole point of letting it be untidy.
